docstring:
**Finite-dimensionality of modular forms.** As a corollary of the Sturm bound, the space
`ModularForm 𝒢 k` is finite-dimensional over `ℂ` for any subgroup `𝒢 ≤ GL(2, ℝ)` of finite
relative index in `𝒮ℒ` with determinant-one elements and discrete strict periods.
description: **Finite-dimensionality of modular forms.** Let $\mathcal{G}$ be a subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}(2,\mathbb{R})$ that has finite index relative to the image of the special linear group $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$, whose elements all have determinant one, and whose group of strict periods is discrete. Then for every integer weight $k$, the space of modular forms of weight $k$ for $\mathcal{G}$ is a finite-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb{C}$.

name: TauCeti.Multiquadratic.not_isSquare_prod_cmRadicand
signature:
theorem TauCeti.Multiquadratic.not_isSquare_prod_cmRadicand : ∀ {ι : Type u_1} (p : ι → ℕ),
  (∀ (i : ι), Nat.Prime (p i)) →
    Function.Injective p →
      ∀ (S : Finset (Option ι)), S.Nonempty → ¬IsSquare (∏ x ∈ S, TauCeti.Multiquadratic.cmRadicand p x)
docstring:
The CM radicand family is square-class independent: for distinct primes `p`, no nonempty
subset product of `-1, p₁, …, pₙ` is a square in `ℚ`.
description: **Square-free independence of the CM radicands.** Let $\iota$ be any index type and let $(p_i)_{i\in\iota}$ be a family of pairwise distinct primes. Define the radicands $\mathrm{cm}(\cdot)$ by sending the index $\ast$ (the `none` case) to $-1$ and each index $i$ to $p_i$. Then for every nonempty finite subset $S$ of $\{\ast\}\cup\iota$, the product of the radicands over $S$ is not a square in $\mathbb{Q}$. Equivalently, no nonempty subproduct of $-1, p_{i_1}, \dots, p_{i_n}$ (with distinct indices) is a rational square.

name: TauCeti.Multiquadratic.ramificationIdx_eq_two_of_liesOver_primeDiscriminantPrime
signature:
theorem TauCeti.Multiquadratic.ramificationIdx_eq_two_of_liesOver_primeDiscriminantPrime : ∀ {ι : Type u} [Finite ι] {L : Type v} [inst : Field L] [inst_1 : NumberField L] (D : ι → ℤ) (root : ι → L),
  (∀ (i : ι), TauCeti.Multiquadratic.IsPrimeDiscriminant (D i)) →
    Function.Injective D →
      (∀ (i j : ι),
          TauCeti.Multiquadratic.IsEvenPrimeDiscriminant (D i) →
            TauCeti.Multiquadratic.IsEvenPrimeDiscriminant (D j) → D i = D j) →
        (∀ (i : ι), root i ^ 2 = (algebraMap ℚ L) ↑(TauCeti.Multiquadratic.primeDiscriminantRadicand (D i))) →
          IntermediateField.adjoin ℚ (Set.range root) = ⊤ →
            ∀ (i : ι) (𝔓 : Ideal (NumberField.RingOfIntegers L)) [𝔓.IsPrime]
              [𝔓.LiesOver (Ideal.span {↑(TauCeti.Multiquadratic.primeDiscriminantPrime (D i))})],
              𝔓.ramificationIdx ℤ = 2
docstring:
**The ramification index at a ramified prime of a prime-discriminant compositum is `2`.**
However many factors the compositum has, a prime belonging to one of them has ramification index
exactly two: the inertia subgroup at a ramified prime is as small as it can be.

The upper bound is transverse cancellation. The compositum `U` of the other roots is unramified at
the prime (`isUnramifiedIn_adjoin_range_ne_primeDiscriminantPrime`), so the absolute ramification
index equals the relative one over `U`, which is at most `[L : U] = 2`. The lower bound is the
total ramification of the quadratic subfield `ℚ(root i)`.
description: **Ramification index at a ramified prime of a prime-discriminant compositum.** Let $\iota$ be a finite index set, let $L$ be a number field, and for each $i \in \iota$ let $D_i$ be a prime discriminant, with the $D_i$ pairwise distinct and at most one of them even. Suppose each $\sqrt{r_i}$ is a root $\alpha_i \in L$ of a rational number $r_i$ whose square root generates the quadratic field attached to $D_i$, and suppose the $\alpha_i$ generate $L$ over $\mathbb{Q}$. Then for every $i \in \iota$ and every prime $\mathfrak{P}$ of the ring of integers of $L$ lying over the prime $p_i$ associated to $D_i$ (namely the prime dividing $D_i$, with $p_i = 2$ in the even case), the ramification index of $\mathfrak{P}$ over $\mathbb{Z}$ is exactly $2$.

name: TauCeti.Multiquadratic.intermediateFieldEquivSubmoduleSqrtPrimes_apply_ofDual_eq
signature:
theorem TauCeti.Multiquadratic.intermediateFieldEquivSubmoduleSqrtPrimes_apply_ofDual_eq : ∀ {ι : Type u_1} [inst : Finite ι] (p : ι → ℕ) (hp : ∀ (i : ι), Nat.Prime (p i)) (hinj : Function.Injective p)
  (F : IntermediateField ℚ ↥(IntermediateField.adjoin ℚ (Set.range fun i => √↑(p i)))),
  OrderDual.ofDual ((TauCeti.Multiquadratic.intermediateFieldEquivSubmoduleSqrtPrimes p hp hinj) F) =
    OrderDual.ofDual ((TauCeti.Multiquadratic.intermediateFieldEquivSubmodule ⋯ ⋯) F)
docstring:
The subspace attached by the public prime-radicand dictionary is extensionally the same as
the generic dictionary fed the prime-family square-class independence proof. This lets consumers
use the degree theorems from `SubfieldDegree` with
`intermediateFieldEquivSubmoduleSqrtPrimes` without a parallel prime-specific degree API.
description: **Equality of the prime-radicand and generic subspace dictionaries.** Let $\iota$ be a finite index type, and let $(p_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a family of primes indexed by $\iota$ that is injective (so the primes are pairwise distinct). Let $K = \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p_i} : i \in \iota)$. For every intermediate field $F$ between $\mathbb{Q}$ and $K$, the subspace associated to $F$ by the dictionary specialized to prime radicands coincides with the subspace associated to $F$ by the generic dictionary, which is built from the square-class independence property proven for the prime family. In other words, the two correspondences from intermediate fields to subspaces agree on every intermediate field (the equality is taken in the order-dual sense, so it is an equality of the underlying subspaces).

name: TauCeti.Multiquadratic.IsNarrowGenusField
signature: structure TauCeti.Multiquadratic.IsNarrowGenusField : ℤ → (L : Type u) → [inst : Field L] → [NumberField L] → L → Prop
docstring:
An abelian extension `L / ℚ`, with a chosen quadratic subfield generated by `y² = d`, is a
**narrow genus field** when it is unramified over that subfield at every finite place and is
maximal among abelian extensions with those properties.

No condition is imposed at infinite places. This is the distinction between the narrow genus
field and the everywhere-unramified genus field for a real quadratic radicand.
description: **Narrow Genus Field.** Let $d$ be an integer, let $L$ be a number field, and let $y \in L$ satisfy $y^2 = d$, so that $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$ sits inside $L$ as a quadratic subfield. The predicate asserts that $L$ is a narrow genus field of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$ in the following sense: $L/\mathbb{Q}$ is an abelian extension, $L/\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$ is unramified at every finite prime (no condition is imposed at the infinite places, so ramification at real places is allowed), and $L$ is maximal with respect to these two properties among abelian extensions of $\mathbb{Q}$. When $d$ is positive, this differs from the everywhere-unramified genus field, which additionally requires unramifiedness at infinite places.

name: TauCeti.GlobalNumberFields.ideleCongruenceSubgroup
signature:
def TauCeti.GlobalNumberFields.ideleCongruenceSubgroup : {K : Type u_1} →
  [inst : Field K] →
    [inst_1 : NumberField K] →
      TauCeti.GlobalNumberFields.Modulus K → Subgroup (NumberField.IdeleGroup (NumberField.RingOfIntegers K) K)
docstring:
**The idele congruence subgroup of a modulus**: the ideles congruent to one modulo `𝔪` that
are moreover units of the valuation ring at the finite places not dividing `𝔪`.  Explicitly, they
are principal units of the prescribed level at the finite divisors of `𝔪`, units of the valuation
ring at the remaining finite places, and positive at the real places selected by `𝔪`.  No
condition is imposed at the infinite places outside `𝔪`.
description:
**Idele congruence subgroup.** Let $K$ be a number field and let $\mathfrak{m}$ be a modulus of $K$ (a formal product of finite primes of $K$, together with a choice of real places). The idele congruence subgroup attached to $\mathfrak{m}$ is the subgroup of the idele group of $K$ consisting of those ideles $x = (x_v)_v$ satisfying the following local conditions:

- At each finite place $v$ dividing $\mathfrak{m}$, the component $x_v$ is a principal unit of the prescribed level, i.e. $x_v \equiv 1$ modulo the corresponding power of $v$.
- At each finite place $v$ not dividing $\mathfrak{m}$, the component $x_v$ is a unit of the valuation ring $\mathcal{O}_v$ (so $x_v \in \mathcal{O}_v^\times$).
- At each real place selected by $\mathfrak{m}$, the component $x_v$ is positive.
- At the infinite places not selected by $\mathfrak{m}$, no condition is imposed.

The statement defines this set as a subgroup of the idele group of $K$, which is the standard congruence subgroup of ideles determined by the modulus $\mathfrak{m}$.

    (TauCeti.GlobalNumberFields.residueSignHom 𝔪) ((TauCeti.GlobalNumberFields.unitsToPrimeToSubgroup 𝔪) u)
description: **Compatibility of the units-residue-sign homomorphism with the restriction map.** Let $K$ be a number field and let $\mathfrak{m}$ be a modulus of $K$. For every unit $u$ in the ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$ (i.e., every element of the unit group $\mathcal{O}_K^\times$), the value of the units-residue-sign homomorphism at $u$ equals the value of the residue-sign homomorphism (attached to $\mathfrak{m}$) evaluated at the image of $u$ under the map $\mathcal{O}_K^\times \to (\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{m})^\times$-type homomorphism that sends a unit to its class prime to the modulus. In other words, the two homomorphisms agree: first viewing $u$ as an element of the group of residues prime to $\mathfrak{m}$ and then applying the residue-sign map gives the same result as applying the units-residue-sign map directly to $u$.

**The Artin automorphism at `v ∉ S` is the Frobenius there.** Any arithmetic Frobenius at any
prime above `v` equals it, which is what makes the assignment `v ↦ artinElementAway hab S hur v`
well defined without a choice of prime above `v`.
description: **Artin automorphism at unramified places is the Frobenius.** Let $K \subseteq L$ be a Galois extension of number fields whose Galois group is abelian, and let $S$ be a finite set of nonzero primes of $\mathcal{O}_K$ such that every prime $v \notin S$ is unramified in $L$ (in the sense that every prime $Q$ of $\mathcal{O}_L$ lying over $v$ is unramified over $\mathcal{O}_K$). Let $v$ be a prime of $\mathcal{O}_K$ not in $S$, and let $Q$ be any prime of $\mathcal{O}_L$ lying over $v$. If $\sigma \in \mathrm{Gal}(L/K)$ is an arithmetic Frobenius element at $Q$, then the Artin automorphism assigned to $v$ (the element $\mathrm{artinElementAway}$ attached to $v$) is equal to $\sigma$. In other words, every arithmetic Frobenius at any prime above $v$ coincides with the Artin symbol of $v$, so the assignment $v \mapsto \sigma_v$ is independent of the choice of prime above $v$.

name: TauCeti.rationalPrimeBelow

docstring:
The rational prime below a height-one prime `𝔭` of `𝓞 K`, that is, the residue
characteristic of `𝔭`.  It is the absolute norm of the prime `𝔭 ∩ ℤ` of `ℤ`.
description: **Rational prime below a prime ideal.** For a number field $K$ and a nonzero prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ of the ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$ (a height-one prime), this assigns the natural number given by the residue characteristic of $\mathfrak{p}$: namely, the rational prime $p$ lying under $\mathfrak{p}$, i.e. the prime with $\mathfrak{p} \cap \mathbb{Z} = p\mathbb{Z}$. Equivalently, it is the absolute norm of the prime ideal $\mathfrak{p} \cap \mathbb{Z}$ of $\mathbb{Z}$.

theorem IsDedekindDomain.HeightOneSpectrum.intCast_mem_asIdeal_iff : ∀ {K : Type u_1} [inst : Field K] (𝔭 : IsDedekindDomain.HeightOneSpectrum (NumberField.RingOfIntegers K)) (n : ℤ),

docstring:
An integer belongs to a height-one prime exactly when the rational prime below it divides that
integer.
description: **Integers lying in a height-one prime.** Let $K$ be a number field, let $\mathfrak{p}$ be a height-one prime (equivalently, a nonzero prime ideal) of the ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$, and let $p$ be the rational prime lying below $\mathfrak{p}$. Then for every integer $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, the integer $n$ (viewed as an element of $\mathcal{O}_K$) belongs to $\mathfrak{p}$ if and only if $p$ divides $n$.

The underlying linear map of the real-place diagonal isometry is the canonical distribution
of tensor product over the finite coordinate space.
description: **Weighted sum of squares at a real place.** Let $K$ be a field, $\iota$ a finite index type, $w$ a real place of $K$, and $a = (a_i)_{i\in\iota}$ a family of elements of $K$. Let $x$ be an element of the real scalar extension of $K$ at $w$. Then the value at $x$ of the quadratic form attached to the weighted sum of squares at $w$ (built from the coefficients $a_i$, viewed through the real embedding of $K$ at $w$) equals the image of $x$ under the canonical map that distributes the tensor product over the finite product $\iota \to \mathbb{R}$, with the $K$-algebra structure on the target given by the real embedding at $w$. theorem TauCeti.Probability.blockLaw_def : ∀ {Ω : Type u_1} {α : Type u_2} {ι : Type u_4} [inst : MeasurableSpace Ω] [inst_1 : MeasurableSpace α]
  (μ : MeasureTheory.Measure Ω) (X : ι → Ω → α) {m : ℕ} (k : Fin m → ι),
  TauCeti.Probability.blockLaw μ X k = MeasureTheory.Measure.map (fun ω i => X (k i) ω) μ
description: **Block law definition.** Let $(\Omega, \mathcal{F})$ and $(\alpha, \mathcal{A})$ be measurable spaces, let $\mu$ be a measure on $\Omega$, let $(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a family of $\alpha$-valued functions on $\Omega$, and let $k = (k_1, \dots, k_m)$ be a finite list of indices from $\iota$. The block law of $(X_i)$ along $k$ with respect to $\mu$ is the image (pushforward) measure of $\mu$ under the map $\omega \mapsto (X_{k_1}(\omega), \dots, X_{k_m}(\omega))$ sending $\Omega$ to $\alpha^m$. In other words, the block law is the distribution of the finite subfamily $(X_{k_i})_{i=1}^m$ under $\mu$.

name: TauCeti.ClassData.classMultMatrix_commute

  (i j : Fin d.numClasses), Commute (d.classMultMatrix i) (d.classMultMatrix j)
docstring:
The numbered class-multiplication matrices commute pairwise, the centre of the group algebra
being commutative.
description: **Commutativity of class-multiplication matrices.** Let $G$ be a finite group equipped with its class data $d$, which consists of $d.\text{numClasses}$ conjugacy-class-type objects indexed by $\{0, \dots, \text{numClasses}-1\}$. For any two indices $i, j$, the class-multiplication matrices $M_i$ and $M_j$ associated to $d$ commute, i.e. $M_i M_j = M_j M_i$. This reflects the fact that the centre of the group algebra $\mathbb{C}[G]$ is commutative.

name: TauCeti.isInvInvariant_haarProb

name: Rep.augmentation

docstring:
The **augmentation** `k[G] ⟶ k`, the map of representations sending a group ring element to
the sum of its coefficients; it is the map out of the left regular representation attached to
`1 : k`.
description: **Augmentation map.** Let $k$ be a commutative ring and $G$ a group. The augmentation is the morphism of $k$-linear representations of $G$ from the left regular representation $k[G]$ (the free $k$-module with basis $G$, with $G$ acting by left multiplication) to the trivial representation $k$ (with $G$ acting trivially). It sends each group ring element $\sum_{g} a_g\, g$ to the sum of its coefficients $\sum_{g} a_g \in k$. Equivalently, it is the representation map determined by sending the basis element $1 \in G$ to $1 \in k$.

docstring: The degree-two component of the bar homotopy for inverse conjugation.
description: **Degree-two bar homotopy for inverse conjugation.** Given a group $K$, a type $A$ equipped with a subtraction operation, an element $g \in K$, a function $f : K \times K \to A$ (a two-variable cochain), and an element $k \in K$, this produces an element of $A$. It is the degree-two component of the bar homotopy used to relate the inverse-conjugation action on continuous cochains of $K$ to the identity, evaluated at the cochain $f$, the parameter $g$, and the point $k$.

name: TauCeti.continuousSMulQuotientFixedPointsOfContinuousSMul
signature:
instance TauCeti.continuousSMulQuotientFixedPointsOfContinuousSMul : ∀ (G : Type u_1) [inst : Group G] [inst_1 : TopologicalSpace G] (M : Type u_2) [inst_2 : AddGroup M]
  [inst_3 : DistribMulAction G M] [inst_4 : TopologicalSpace M] [DiscreteTopology M] [ContinuousSMul G M]
  (H : Subgroup G) [inst_7 : H.Normal], ContinuousSMul (G ⧸ H) ↥(FixedPoints.addSubgroup (↥H) M)
docstring:
For an arbitrary normal subgroup `H`, the action of `G ⧸ H` on the invariants `M ^ H` of a
discrete module is continuous. Unlike
`TauCeti.continuousSMulQuotientFixedPoints`, which reads the continuity off the discreteness of
`G ⧸ H` for open `H` and needs no continuity of the `G`-action, this deduces it from continuity of
the `G`-action: the invariants are discrete, so continuity is continuity in the group variable
alone, and there it is the continuity of the `G`-action read through the quotient map. No
compatibility of the topology of `G` with its group structure is needed, since `G ⧸ H` carries the
quotient topology.
description: **Continuity of the induced action on invariants under a normal subgroup.** Let $G$ be a topological group (a group carrying a topology, with no compatibility assumed between the topology and the group operations), let $M$ be an additive group with a discrete topology, and suppose $G$ acts on $M$ by distributive actions such that the action map $G \times M \to M$ is continuous. Let $H$ be a normal subgroup of $G$. Then the quotient group $G/H$ acts on the subgroup $M^H$ of $H$-invariant elements of $M$, and this action is continuous when $G/H$ is given the quotient topology and $M^H$ carries the subspace topology inherited from $M$ (which is discrete). In other words, for every $G/H$-action on $M^H$ coming from the $G$-action, the scalar multiplication $(G/H) \times M^H \to M^H$ is continuous.

description: **Tate cohomology in degree −1 for finite cyclic groups.** Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $G$ a finite group, and $M$ a representation of $G$ over $R$. Suppose $g \in G$ is an element generating $G$ (every element of $G$ is a power of $g$), and note that $-1$ is odd. Then the comparison isomorphism $\widehat{H}^{-1}(G, M) \cong$ (the odd-degree comparison isomorphism, specialized to degree $-1$) coincides with the isomorphism $\text{tateCohomologyIsoNegOne}$ defined directly in degree $-1$. In other words, for a finite cyclic group, the general odd-degree Tate cohomology identification, evaluated at degree $-1$, agrees with the dedicated degree $-1$ identification.

name: TauCeti.conjNormalFDRepEquiv

Conjugation by `g` is an autoequivalence of `FDRep k N`, with inverse conjugation by `g⁻¹`:
Mathlib's `Action.resEquiv` for the automorphism `MulAut.conjNormal g⁻¹` of `N`.

The body is sealed, as for `conjNormalRepEquiv`; `conjNormalFDRepEquiv_functor` and
`conjNormalFDRepEquiv_inverse` are the interface identifying it with conjugation.
description: **Conjugation autoequivalence on normal-subgroup representations.** Let $k$ be a ring, $G$ a group, and $N$ a normal subgroup of $G$. For each element $g \in G$, conjugation by $g$ gives an autoequivalence of the category of finite-dimensional representations of $N$ over $k$. Explicitly, this is an equivalence of categories from this category to itself, whose inverse is given by conjugation by $g^{-1}$. It is obtained by restricting along the automorphism of $N$ given by conjugation by $g^{-1}$.

name: TauCeti.ClassFunction.indVirtualCharacters

def TauCeti.ClassFunction.indVirtualCharacters : (k : Type u) →

**The virtual characters of `G` induced from a family of subgroups**: the additive subgroup of
`G → k` generated by `Ind_S^G ψ` for `S` satisfying `P` and `ψ` a virtual character of `S`.

For `P` the cyclic or elementary subgroups this is the subgroup generated by induction from their
virtual-character lattices; it is the image of the induction map `⨁_S R(S) → R(G)`.
description: **Subgroup of virtual characters induced from a family of subgroups.** Let $k$ be a field and $G$ a finite group, and let $P$ be a property of subgroups of $G$. This defines an additive subgroup of the group of $k$-valued class functions on $G$ (functions $G \to k$). It is the additive subgroup generated by all induced class functions $\operatorname{Ind}_S^G \psi$, where $S$ ranges over subgroups of $G$ satisfying $P$ and $\psi$ ranges over virtual characters of $S$. In particular, when $P$ picks out the cyclic subgroups (or the elementary subgroups), this is the subgroup obtained by inducing the virtual character lattices of those subgroups up to $G$; equivalently, it is the image of the induction map $\bigoplus_S R(S) \to R(G)$.

theorem TauCeti.Representation.isIrreducible_of_linearEquiv : ∀ {k : Type u_1} {G : Type u_2} {V : Type u_3} [inst : Field k] [inst_1 : Monoid G] [inst_2 : AddCommGroup V]
  [inst_3 : Module k V] {W : Type u_4} [inst_4 : AddCommGroup W] [inst_5 : Module k W] {ρ : Representation k G V}
  {σ : Representation k G W} (e : V ≃ₗ[k] W),

docstring:
**Irreducibility transports along an equivariant linear equivalence.** A linear equivalence
intertwining two representations matches their lattices of subrepresentations, by taking preimages
of invariant subspaces, so one is irreducible exactly when the other is.

Only one direction is stated; the reverse is this one applied to `e.symm`.
description: **Irreducibility is preserved under equivariant linear isomorphism.** Let $k$ be a field, $G$ a monoid, and $V$, $W$ vector spaces over $k$. Let $\rho$ be a representation of $G$ on $V$ and $\sigma$ a representation of $G$ on $W$, and let $e : V \to W$ be a $k$-linear isomorphism such that $e(\rho(g)v) = \sigma(g)(e(v))$ for all $g \in G$ and $v \in V$. Then if $\rho$ is irreducible, $\sigma$ is irreducible.

**Finite-dimensionality of the path algebra is acyclicity of the quiver**, the reading of
`TauCeti.module_finite_pathAlgebra_iff_isAcyclic` over a division ring.
description: **Finite-dimensionality of path algebras characterizes acyclic quivers.** Let $k$ be a division ring and let $Q$ be a finite quiver (finitely many vertices and finitely many arrows between any two vertices). Then the path algebra $kQ$ of $Q$ over $k$ is finite-dimensional as a $k$-vector space if and only if the quiver $Q$ is acyclic, meaning it contains no oriented cycles.

docstring:
**The projection `P₁ ↠ S₁` is the identification of the two lines at the source**, read through
`TauCeti.simpleRepSelfEquiv` and `TauCeti.kroneckerProjSrcEquiv`.
description: **Projection onto the simple at the source.** Let $k$ be a field and $A$ a type with exactly one element, so the Kronecker quiver has a single arrow from the source vertex to the target vertex. Take any element $y$ of the underlying vector space at the source vertex of the indecomposable projective representation $P_1$. Then applying the component at the source vertex of the map $g$ in the Auslander–Reiten sequence, and then identifying the resulting space with the simple representation $S_1$ at the source, gives the same value as applying the canonical projection $P_1 \twoheadrightarrow S_1$ at the source to $y$. In other words, the two ways of sending $P_1$ to $S_1$ at the source agree, since both identify the one-dimensional source line.

name: TauCeti.kroneckerLineRepScalar_intertwine
signature:
theorem TauCeti.kroneckerLineRepScalar_intertwine : ∀ {k : Type u} [inst : Field k] {A : Type v} {a₁ : A} {c d : k} [Nontrivial A]
  (e : TauCeti.kroneckerLineRep k a₁ c ⟶ TauCeti.kroneckerLineRep k a₁ d),
  c * TauCeti.kroneckerLineRepScalar e = d * TauCeti.kroneckerLineRepScalar e
docstring:
**On a quiver carrying more than one arrow the scalars of the two lines agree on the scalar of
any morphism between them**, by naturality along the distinguished arrow. The hypothesis
`Nontrivial A` is the existence of an arrow other than the distinguished one: it forces the two
components of the morphism to agree.
description: **Scalar agreement for morphisms between Kronecker line representations.** Let $k$ be a field, $A$ a nontrivial type (so that there exists an arrow of the quiver other than a fixed distinguished one), and $a_1 \in A$ the distinguished arrow. For any scalars $c, d \in k$ and any morphism $e$ from the Kronecker line representation with parameter $c$ to the Kronecker line representation with parameter $d$ (both built on the distinguished arrow $a_1$), the scalar attached to $e$ satisfies $c\cdot \lambda(e) = d\cdot \lambda(e)$, where $\lambda(e)$ denotes the scalar of the morphism $e$. Equivalently, $(c-d)\,\lambda(e) = 0$.

name: Rep.simple_iff_isIrreducible
signature:
theorem Rep.simple_iff_isIrreducible : ∀ {k : Type u} {G : Type v} [inst : Field k] [inst_1 : Monoid G] (A : Rep.{w, u, v} k G),
  CategoryTheory.Simple A ↔ A.ρ.IsIrreducible
docstring:
**An object of `Rep k G` is simple exactly when the representation it carries is
irreducible.** Both sides say that the `k[G]`-module the object carries is simple: the left-hand
side across `Rep.equivalenceModuleMonoidAlgebra`, the right-hand side across
`Representation.irreducible_iff_isSimpleModule_asModule`.
description:
**Simple objects of representations are irreducible representations.** Let $k$ be a field and $G$ a monoid (in particular, a group may be considered). For any representation $A$ of $G$ over $k$, the following are equivalent:

- $A$ is a simple object in the category of representations of $G$ over $k$ (it is nonzero and has no proper nonzero subrepresentations);
- the underlying representation $\rho$ of $A$ is irreducible, i.e. $A$ has no nontrivial $G$-invariant $k$-subspaces.

Equivalently, viewing $A$ as a module over the monoid algebra $k[G]$, this says that $A$ is a simple $k[G]$-module.

name: Subrepresentation.toRepresentation_apply
signature:
theorem Subrepresentation.toRepresentation_apply : ∀ {A : Type u_1} {G : Type u_2} {W : Type u_3} [inst : Semiring A] [inst_1 : Monoid G] [inst_2 : AddCommMonoid W]
  [inst_3 : Module A W] {ρ : Representation A G W} (S : Subrepresentation ρ) (g : G),
  S.toRepresentation g = (ρ g).restrict ⋯
docstring: The action on a subrepresentation is the restriction of the original action.
description: **Restriction of the action on a subrepresentation.** Let $A$ be a semiring, $G$ a monoid, and $W$ an $A$-module, and let $\rho$ be a representation of $G$ on $W$ over $A$. For any subrepresentation $S$ of $\rho$ (an $A$-submodule of $W$ invariant under every $\rho(g)$) and any element $g \in G$, the induced representation of $g$ on $S$ coincides with the restriction of the linear map $\rho(g)$ to $S$; that is, acting by $g$ on $S$ is the same as applying $\rho(g)$ and viewing the result as an element of $S$.

name: TauCeti.permConjClassPartition_partitionEquivConjClasses
signature: theorem TauCeti.permConjClassPartition_partitionEquivConjClasses : ∀ (n : ℕ) (p : n.Partition), TauCeti.permConjClassPartition ((TauCeti.partitionEquivConjClasses n) p) = (Equiv.cast ⋯) p
docstring: The conjugacy class associated to a partition of `n` has that partition.
description: **Conjugacy classes recover their partitions.** For every natural number $n$ and every partition $p$ of $n$, take the conjugacy class of permutations in the symmetric group on $n$ points that corresponds to $p$ under the standard bijection between partitions of $n$ and conjugacy classes. Then the partition associated with that conjugacy class (by cycle type) is exactly $p$. In other words, the map sending a conjugacy class to its cycle-type partition is a left inverse of the bijection from partitions to conjugacy classes.

name: TauCeti.spechtModule_ones_ρ_apply
signature:
theorem TauCeti.spechtModule_ones_ρ_apply : ∀ (n : ℕ) (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) (x : ↑(TauCeti.spechtModule (TauCeti.Nat.Partition.ones n)).V),
  ((TauCeti.spechtModule (TauCeti.Nat.Partition.ones n)).ρ σ) x = ↑↑(Equiv.Perm.sign σ) • x
docstring:
**`S^{(1ⁿ)}` is the sign representation**: the symmetric group acts on it through the sign
character.  The sign is unchanged by the relabelling `Fin n ≃ Fin (diagramOf (1ⁿ)).card` that
`TauCeti.spechtModule` transports along.

This is not a `simp` lemma, for the reason given at
`TauCeti.spechtModule_indiscrete_ρ_apply`.
description: **Sign representation for the partition $(1^n)$.** For every natural number $n$, every permutation $\sigma$ of an $n$-element set, and every vector $x$ in the underlying space of the Specht module attached to the partition $(1^n)$ of $n$ (the partition into $n$ parts each equal to $1$), the action of $\sigma$ on $x$ is multiplication by the sign of $\sigma$, i.e. $\rho(\sigma)x = \operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\, x$, where $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma) \in \{1,-1\}$ is viewed as a scalar in the base field. In other words, the Specht module $S^{(1^n)}$ is the sign representation of the symmetric group.

name: TauCeti.youngSubgroup
signature: def TauCeti.youngSubgroup : {n : ℕ} → n.Partition → Subgroup (Equiv.Perm (Fin n))
docstring:
The Young subgroup associated to `μ`, acting independently on the consecutive blocks whose
sizes are the decreasing parts of `μ`.
description: **Young subgroup.** Given a natural number $n$ and a partition $\mu$ of $n$, the Young subgroup of $\mu$ is the subgroup of the symmetric group $S_n$ (permutations of $\{1,\dots,n\}$) obtained by splitting $\{1,\dots,n\}$ into consecutive blocks whose sizes are the parts of $\mu$ (taken in decreasing order), and consisting of all permutations that map each block to itself. Equivalently, it is the product $S_{\mu_1}\times S_{\mu_2}\times\cdots$ of symmetric groups acting independently on these consecutive blocks.

name: IsHausdorff.pi
signature:
instance IsHausdorff.pi : ∀ {R : Type u_1} [inst : CommRing R] (I : Ideal R) {ι : Type u_2} (M : ι → Type u_3)
  [inst_1 : (i : ι) → AddCommGroup (M i)] [inst_2 : (i : ι) → Module R (M i)] [∀ (i : ι), IsHausdorff I (M i)],
  IsHausdorff I ((i : ι) → M i)
docstring: A product of `I`-adically Hausdorff modules is `I`-adically Hausdorff.
description: **Product of $I$-adically Hausdorff modules.** Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $I$ an ideal of $R$, and let $\{M_i\}_{i\in\iota}$ be a family of $R$-modules, each $I$-adically Hausdorff (i.e., $\bigcap_{n\ge 1} I^n M_i = 0$ for every $i$). Then the product module $\prod_{i\in\iota} M_i$ is also $I$-adically Hausdorff, meaning that its intersection $\bigcap_{n\ge 1} I^n \prod_{i\in\iota} M_i$ consists only of the zero element.

name: Algebra.GrothendieckAddGroup.ofRingHom
signature: def Algebra.GrothendieckAddGroup.ofRingHom : {S : Type u_3} → [inst : NonAssocSemiring S] → S →+* Algebra.GrothendieckAddGroup S
docstring: The canonical map from a semiring into its Grothendieck ring.
description: **Canonical map into the Grothendieck ring.** For any (non-associative) semiring $S$, there is a canonical ring homomorphism from $S$ into its Grothendieck ring, sending each element $s \in S$ to its class in the Grothendieck construction. This map is additive and multiplicative and preserves the identity element, so it realizes $S$ as a sub-semiring-like object inside its Grothendieck ring.

name: TauCeti.Huber.PairOfDefinition.rationalQuotientRingEquiv_quotientMk_weightedX
signature:
theorem TauCeti.Huber.PairOfDefinition.rationalQuotientRingEquiv_quotientMk_weightedX : ∀ {A : Type u_1} [inst : CommRing A] [inst_1 : UniformSpace A] [inst_2 : IsUniformAddGroup A]
  [inst_3 : IsTopologicalRing A] [inst_4 : TauCeti.Huber.IsHuberRing A] [inst_5 : CompleteSpace A]
  (P : TauCeti.Huber.PairOfDefinition A) (T : Finset A) (s : A) (S : Type u_2) [inst_6 : CommRing S]
  [inst_7 : Algebra A S] [inst_8 : IsLocalization.Away s S] (hden : P.HasDenominatorPower T s S) {k : ℕ} (t : Fin k → A)
  (ht : ∀ (i : Fin k), t i ∈ T) (hsplit : ∀ u ∈ T, u = s ∨ u ∈ Set.range t) (hspan : Ideal.span (insert s ↑T) = ⊤)
  (hcl : IsClosed ↑(TauCeti.Huber.rationalRelationIdeal t s)) (i : Fin k),
  (P.rationalQuotientRingEquiv T s S hden t ht hsplit hspan hcl)
      ((Ideal.Quotient.mk (TauCeti.Huber.rationalRelationIdeal t s)) (TauCeti.Huber.weightedX (fun x => {1}) ⋯ i)) =
    ↑(TauCeti.Localization.divBy (t i) s)
docstring:
**The identification sends `Xᵢ` to `tᵢ/s`**: the class of the variable goes to the image in
`A⟨T/s⟩` of the fraction `divBy (t i) s`. The inverse form is
`rationalQuotientRingEquiv_symm_coe_divBy`.
description: **Quotient-variable identification in the rational localization.** Let $A$ be a complete, uniform, topological commutative ring that is a Huber ring, let $P$ be a pair of definition for $A$, let $T$ be a finite subset of $A$, and let $s \in A$ with $S$ the localization of $A$ at $s$, where $P$ has denominator power $T$ and $s$ relative to $S$. Let $t_1,\dots,t_k$ be elements of $A$ lying in $T$, such that every element of $T$ is either $s$ or one of the $t_i$, the ideal generated by $\{s\} \cup T$ is the whole ring, and the ideal of relations associated to $(t_i)$ and $s$ is closed. Then the isomorphism from the rational quotient ring (built from this data) to $S$-side algebra sends the class of the $i$-th weighted variable $X_i$ (taken in the quotient by the relation ideal) to the fraction $t_i/s$, i.e. the element $\mathrm{divBy}(t_i, s)$ in the localization $A\langle T/s\rangle$.

name: TauCeti.transcendental_of_D_ne_zero
signature:
theorem TauCeti.transcendental_of_D_ne_zero : ∀ {k : Type u_1} {F : Type u_2} [inst : Field k] [inst_1 : Field F] [inst_2 : Algebra k F] {x : F} [PerfectField k],
  (KaehlerDifferential.D k F) x ≠ 0 → Transcendental k x
docstring:
Over a perfect base field, an element with nonzero universal differential is transcendental:
an algebraic element is separable, hence has vanishing differential.
description: **Transcendence criterion via universal derivation.** Let $k$ be a perfect field and $F$ a field containing $k$ as a subfield. For any element $x \in F$, if the value $d_k(x)$ of the universal derivation $d_k : F \to \Omega_{F/k}$ at $x$ is nonzero, then $x$ is transcendental over $k$. Equivalently, every element of $F$ that is algebraic over $k$ has vanishing universal differential.

name: TauCeti.BoundedSSYT.sum_weight
signature: theorem TauCeti.BoundedSSYT.sum_weight : ∀ {N : ℕ} {μ : YoungDiagram} (T : TauCeti.BoundedSSYT N μ), ∑ i, T.weight i = μ.card
docstring:
The sum of the weight of a bounded tableau of shape `μ` is the number of cells of `μ`: every
cell carries exactly one letter.
description: **Total weight of a bounded semistandard Young tableau.** For every natural number $N$, every Young diagram $\mu$, and every bounded semistandard Young tableau $T$ of shape $\mu$ with entries bounded by $N$, the weight of $T$ summed over all letters $i$ (that is, the total count of entries of each value, taken over all possible letters) equals the number of cells of $\mu$. This reflects the fact that each cell of the tableau contains exactly one letter, so the letter counts add up to the size of the diagram.

name: Valuation.characteristicSubgroup_eq_comap_of_isEquiv
docstring: Equality form of the invariance: `cΓ_v` is the pullback of `cΓ_w`.
description: **Invariance of the characteristic subgroup under equivalence.** Let $A$ be a ring, and let $v : A \to \Gamma_0$ and $w : A \to \Gamma_0'$ be two valuations with values in linearly ordered commutative groups with zero. If $v$ and $w$ are equivalent, then the characteristic subgroup of $v$ is exactly the preimage of the characteristic subgroup of $w$ under the order isomorphism between the value groups of $v$ and $w$ that equivalence provides. In other words, the characteristic subgroup attached to $v$ is the pullback, along this isomorphism, of the one attached to $w$.

name: TauCeti.valuativeExtension_self
signature: instance TauCeti.valuativeExtension_self : ∀ (K : Type u_1) [inst : CommSemiring K] [inst_1 : ValuativeRel K], ValuativeExtension K K
docstring: A commutative semiring equipped with a valuative relation is a valuative extension of itself.
description: **Every commutative semiring equipped with a valuative relation is a valuative extension of itself.** Let $K$ be a commutative semiring carrying a valuative relation. Then $K$, viewed as an extension of itself via the identity map, satisfies the defining conditions of a valuative extension, so the identity $K \to K$ is a valuative extension.

name: TauCeti.gradedMkZero_mul
signature:
theorem TauCeti.gradedMkZero_mul : ∀ {p : ℕ} {G : Type u} [inst : Group G] [inst_1 : TopologicalSpace G] [inst_2 : IsTopologicalGroup G] (g h : G),
  TauCeti.gradedMkZero p G (g * h) = TauCeti.gradedMkZero p G g + TauCeti.gradedMkZero p G h
description: **Multiplicativity of the degree-zero map.** For every natural number $p$ and every topological group $G$, the map associated with $p$ and $G$ (taking elements of $G$ to the degree-zero graded part) turns the group product into a sum: for all $g, h \in G$, the image of $gh$ equals the sum of the images of $g$ and $h$. In other words, the map is a homomorphism from $G$ to an additive group.

name: TauCeti.gradedPow_gradedBracket_right
signature:
theorem TauCeti.gradedPow_gradedBracket_right : ∀ {p : ℕ} {G : Type u} [inst : Group G] [inst_1 : TopologicalSpace G] [inst_2 : IsTopologicalGroup G] {j k : ℕ},
  1 ≤ k →
    ∀ (x : TauCeti.gradedPiece p G j) (y : TauCeti.gradedPiece p G k),
      TauCeti.gradedPow p G (j + k + 1) (((TauCeti.gradedBracket p G j k) x) y) =
        TauCeti.gradedCast p G ⋯ (((TauCeti.gradedBracket p G j (k + 1)) x) (TauCeti.gradedPow p G k y))
docstring:
**`π` against the bracket on the right**, away from degree zero: `π [x, y] = [x, π y]` for
`y ∈ gr_k(G)` with `k ≥ 1`.
description: **Compatibility of the graded $p$-power map with the bracket.** For every $k \ge 1$, and for all $x$ in the graded piece of degree $j$ and $y$ in the graded piece of degree $k$, applying the $p$-power map to the bracket $[x,y]$ (which lies in degree $j+k$, so its image lies in degree $j+k+1$) gives the same result as taking the bracket of $x$ with $y^p$ (which lies in degree $k+1$, so the bracket lies in degree $j+k+1$), after the canonical degree cast. In symbols, $\pi([x,y]) = [x, \pi(y)]$ under this identification, where $\pi$ denotes the $p$-power map on graded pieces.

name: TauCeti.IsCompactModule.isTopologicalAddGroup
signature:
theorem TauCeti.IsCompactModule.isTopologicalAddGroup : ∀ {R : Type u_1} {M : Type u_2} [inst : Ring R] [inst_1 : AddCommGroup M] [inst_2 : Module R M]
  [inst_3 : TopologicalSpace M] [inst_4 : TopologicalSpace R], TauCeti.IsCompactModule R M → IsTopologicalAddGroup M
docstring: the module is a topological additive group
description: **Compact modules are topological additive groups.** Let $R$ be a ring and $M$ an additive commutative group that is an $R$-module, with topologies on both $R$ and $M$. If $M$ satisfies the compact-module condition, then $M$ with its given topology is a topological additive group, meaning that addition $(x,y)\mapsto x+y$ and negation $x\mapsto -x$ are continuous.

name: TauCeti.TopTriple.Hom.snd
signature: def TauCeti.TopTriple.Hom.snd : {T T' : TauCeti.TopTriple} → (T ⟶ T') → (T.snd ⟶ T'.snd)
docstring: The map between the middle spaces induced by a morphism of triples.
description: **Middle-component map of a morphism of triples.** Given two topological triples $T$ and $T'$ and a morphism $f\colon T \to T'$ between them, this construction produces the induced morphism between their middle components, going from the middle space of $T$ to the middle space of $T'$.

name: TauCeti.AmbientIsotopy.totalHomeomorph_symm_fst
signature:
theorem TauCeti.AmbientIsotopy.totalHomeomorph_symm_fst : ∀ {Y : Type u_2} [inst : TopologicalSpace Y] (Φ : TauCeti.AmbientIsotopy Y) (p : ↑unitInterval × Y),
  (Φ.totalHomeomorph.symm p).1 = p.1
docstring: The inverse total homeomorphism preserves the time coordinate.
description: **Inverse Total Homeomorphism Preserves Time.** Let $Y$ be a topological space and let $\Phi$ be an ambient isotopy of $Y$, indexed by the unit interval $[0,1]$. Its total homeomorphism is a homeomorphism of $[0,1] \times Y$ that sends each pair $(t, y)$ to $(t, \Phi_t(y))$, so it preserves the time coordinate. The statement asserts that the inverse of this homeomorphism also preserves the time coordinate: for every point $(t, y)$ in $[0,1] \times Y$, the time component of the image of $(t, y)$ under the inverse map equals $t$.

name: TauCeti.piCurryHomeomorph_apply
signature:
theorem TauCeti.piCurryHomeomorph_apply : ∀ {ι : Type u_1} {κ : ι → Type u_2} (Y : (i : ι) → κ i → Type u_3)
  [inst : (i : ι) → (j : κ i) → TopologicalSpace (Y i j)] (f : (p : (i : ι) × κ i) → Y p.fst p.snd) (i : ι) (j : κ i),
  (TauCeti.piCurryHomeomorph Y) f i j = f ⟨i, j⟩
description: **Evaluation of the Currying Homeomorphism.** Let $\iota$ be an index type, let $\kappa_i$ be an index type for each $i \in \iota$, and let $Y_{i,j}$ be a topological space for each pair $(i,j)$ with $j \in \kappa_i$. Then the currying homeomorphism $\Pi_{(i,j)} Y_{i,j} \to \Pi_i \Pi_{j \in \kappa_i} Y_{i,j}$ sends a dependent function $f$ on the sigma-type of pairs $(i,j)$ to the map $i \mapsto (j \mapsto f(i,j))$. The statement asserts that for every such $f$ and every $i \in \iota$ and $j \in \kappa_i$, the value of the curried function at $i$ and then $j$ equals $f(i,j)$.

name: TauCeti.IsUniformlyLocallyConnected
signature: def TauCeti.IsUniformlyLocallyConnected : {X : Type u_1} → [PseudoMetricSpace X] → Set X → Prop
docstring:
A set `s` is **uniformly locally connected** if for every `ε > 0` there is a `δ > 0` such that
any two points of `s` at distance less than `δ` are joined by a connected subset of `s` of diameter
at most `ε`.

The smallness of the joining set is spelled out as a pairwise distance bound rather than as
`Metric.diam C ≤ ε`, because `Metric.diam` is `0` on an unbounded set, which would let an unbounded
`C` satisfy the condition vacuously. The lemma
`TauCeti.IsUniformlyLocallyConnected.exists_isConnected_diam_le` recovers the diameter phrasing,
boundedness of the joining set being one of its consequences.
description: **Uniform local connectedness.** A subset $s$ of a pseudometric space $X$ is uniformly locally connected if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $\delta > 0$ such that any two points $x, y \in s$ with $d(x,y) < \delta$ lie in a common connected subset $C \subseteq s$ in which any two points are at distance at most $\varepsilon$. Here the smallness of $C$ is expressed as this pairwise distance bound, not as a bound on the diameter, so that unbounded sets cannot satisfy the condition vacuously.
